thread.title: Architect lays out Ft. Getty possibilities
thread.title_full: Architect lays out Ft. Getty possibilities

author: ohtadmin
title: Architect lays out Ft. Getty possibilities
text:
The ad hoc committee tasked with exploring the future of Fort Getty was presented with a preliminary report by the landscape architect hired to analyze the use of the 41-acre park.
Arek Galle, of the Beta Group, delivered his report Tuesday to the committee. He said the intrinsic value of the park is provided by the ocean views, shoreline access and marsh vistas.
“We all know this,” he said. “People come here for the natural character. … That interface with the ocean is the reason why people are here.”
Galle said nearly half of the park, 19 acres, essentially is inaccessible due to its environment. The accessible areas comprise the waterfront (1.8 acres), RV campground (5.9 acres), grassland (3 acres), sailing campus (1.6 acres), overflow parking (1.2 acres), boat and trailer parking (0.63 acres), tent camping (2.8 acres), fortifications (1.1 acres), pavilion (0.91 acres) and roadways (3 acres). That includes 1.25 miles of beaches and a half mile of trails. Only 9 miles, moreover, are completely under municipal control.
“We’re really starting to see how the land is being utilized,” he said. “You start to get a sense of how valuable each of these pieces are. There’s not a lot of land.”
One limitation is that any work within 200 feet from the shoreline must be approved by the state’s Coastal Resources Management Council.
“It doesn’t mean we can’t work on the edges or make improvements,” he said. “But considerations are tighter.”
The park, moreover, could become smaller when considering two feet of sea-level rise by 2100. Galle said Fort Getty could become “an isolated island in the future without some considerations.”
“Not a big surprise,” he said. “I think we’re all aware of it. The topography sets the stage.”
Galle suggested improving the area dominated by Battery Tousard, which he called “the command center” of the park.
“It’s a significant structure,” he said. “In some ways it kind of divides the park in half.”
Galle said the animals living in the battery and the dense vegetation “impede access” to the acre-sized area, which is “probably the highest and most interesting land on the site.” This condition was inherited from the U.S. Army.
“They didn’t know how to make it work,” he said. “It’s complicated so it’s become overgrown. It’s a huge repository for invasive plants. There’s not a lot of habitat.”
Although Galle said he was not proposing an answer for the “underappreciated” battery and its “spectacular views,” he said the committee has been given the opportunity to rethink that area.
“It’s a significant piece of what we have to work with,” he said. “I think it’s too big not to be able to think about what might be able to happen to at least some portion.”
Galle divided the campground into six sections for his presentation. While the average was 4,038 square feet, the six sites in the northeastern section “skewed our average space.” Those sites average 7,500 square feet compared to the 2,361-square-foot sites in the westernmost row.
Committee Chairwoman Marisa Quinn asked about the park in the offseason when the campers depart. She called it “very unattractive.”
“Yeah, I think there’s room for improvement,” Galle said.
“That’s for sure,” replied Quinn.
Galle, however, said “most of us like the offseason” at the campground due to its solitude and views. He was hesitant about recommending significant development in the area.
“It’s largely an open profile with plantings at the edges,” he said. “I think if we go into the center and add some definition. We just have to be cautious.”
Galle said it was “a matter of finding the balance.”
“When the campers are there, it’s a very different space, too,” he said. “It doesn’t feel welcoming at all. Not everybody feels like it is accessible.”
Quinn, however, disagreed.
“I don’t think that’s a problem,” she said. “It’s like a neighborhood.”
Galle also mentioned the possibility of a playground and a smaller pavilion with a couple of picnic tables for families that don’t need the larger structure. Quinn and board member Richard Smith, however, had concerns about that idea.
“There should be no more permanent structures,” Smith said. “Everybody wants open space. It would be contradicting what people are asking for if you add another permanent structure.”
“I agree with that,” Quinn added. “I don’t know what the survey says. I think this survey will be one tool we’ll use when we are developing our recommendations. Personally, I get nervous about additional permanent structures, whether they are benches or a pavilion.”
Quinn, however, asked about whether Galle was considering changes to the “rustic, rocky,” beaches. She mentioned a float “in the middle of the water that we could jump off like at “Green’s Pier.”
While Galle has not yet thoroughly reviewed the beaches, he said, “I think everyone appreciates the sense of wildness on those edges. I’d be careful not to lose that.”
The committee then asked how they could relay their ideas for the February meeting.
“What’s nice is if you bring your ideas on a piece of paper to the session,” Galle said. “We don’t need to see them necessarily in advance because we’re going to work on them together. We’re comfortable working with real-time input. I think you need to hear each other’s perspectives. We’re prepared to talk about it at the table. Sit down and try to coalesce it. If it means we need to continue at the next session, that’s OK.”
Galle said the discussion at the next meeting should focus on the bigger picture.
“We’re probably not going to talk about benches or trash in great detail,” he said. “What if a 5 percent reduction in campers yields another acre of open land? Those are the conversations we need to work through. Or can we give another acre because we found an acre on the top of the battery that we are going to program differently? Now, maybe, we have more land for campers.”
